How to use radio promotion to support a tour

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 2 min read Comparisons & strategy

On this page
  • Define the outcome before building the list
  • Qualify stations for this goal
  • Prepare the assets
  • Campaign timeline
  • Pitch structure
  • Goal-specific scorecard

Tour support gives a radio pitch a concrete reason to exist now. Instead of asking a programmer to care about a release in the abstract, you can connect the music to a date, venue, local audience, and possible interview. The campaign still starts with programming fit; the tour date adds timeliness.

Define the outcome before building the list

Decide whether each market pitch primarily seeks airplay, an interview, a session, a calendar mention, or a ticket giveaway. The right contact changes with the outcome.

  • Airplay before the date from a genre or local-music host
  • A short remote or in-studio interview
  • A calendar listing or event mention from an appropriate local program
  • A ticket giveaway arranged with the venue and station
  • A live session when travel, setup, and station capacity genuinely align

Choose one primary outcome per pitch. Asking for rotation, an interview, a premiere, a session, and a ticket giveaway in the same first email makes every option harder to process.

Qualify stations for this goal

Start with confirmed dates. For each city, find shows that play the genre and have enough lead time to use the story. A small relevant community show is a better target than a major station with no matching program.

  1. Confirm the station or show is active through a current schedule or playlist.
  2. Identify the person who controls the desired outcome.
  3. Read the published submission or booking instructions.
  4. Record a specific reason the release and goal fit.
  5. Verify the contact against the official site before sending.

Prepare the assets

  • Confirmed date, venue, ticket URL, age restriction, and billing
  • One focus track plus a clean radio edit
  • A 50-word tour bio and a market-specific sentence
  • Interview availability with time zone and contact number
  • Approved ticket quantity and terms if proposing a giveaway

Keep assets behind one stable link and make the relevant item obvious. Do not attach large audio or video files unless requested.

Campaign timeline

Begin research four to six weeks before the date and send the first priority pitches about three weeks out. National tours can be worked in route order so imminent markets receive attention first.

WindowAction
PlanningResearch shows, verify contacts, prepare versions and the one-sheet.
First waveSend a small group of individually addressed, high-fit pitches.
Follow-upReply to requests quickly; follow up once after seven to ten days.
ResultConfirm public evidence, thank supporters, and update the next wave.

Pitch structure

Subject: “[Artist] in [City] on [date] — [genre] for [show].” Open with the program fit, state the date and venue, link one track, and make one realistic offer. Never announce a giveaway before the venue and station agree.

Use truthful sender details, a descriptive subject, one clear link, and an easy way to decline future contact. Never buy guaranteed editorial outcomes or continue contacting someone who objects.

Goal-specific scorecard

  • Qualified shows per tour market
  • Interview, session, and giveaway confirmations
  • Verified spins in the three weeks before each show
  • Referral traffic or ticket activity where trackable
  • New presenter relationships preserved for the next visit

After the date, thank the presenter and share a concise outcome only if useful. The long-term value is becoming a known, reliable artist when the route returns.

Frequently asked questions

How far before a tour date should I pitch radio?

Research four to six weeks out and send priority pitches about three weeks before the show. Some interview and session programs need more lead time, so follow their published guidance.

Should I offer free tickets?

Only after the venue, promoter, and station approve the quantity and process. A giveaway can create useful programming, but never promise inventory you do not control.

Can a first tour get radio support?

Yes, especially from local, college, community, and specialty shows when the music fits. Keep the ask realistic and make remote interviews easy.
